paragraphs.heading: What bias means
paragraphs.text: The bias of an estimator is the gap between the value it gives on average, called its expected value, and the true value of the parameter it is trying to estimate. The average here is taken over all the observations that could possibly turn up. An estimator with zero bias is called unbiased. In statistics, bias is an objective property of the estimator itself.

paragraphs.heading: Why small bias is tolerated
paragraphs.text: Other things being equal, an unbiased estimator is better than a biased one. In practice, though, biased estimators with small bias are used often, and when one is used, bounds on its bias are worked out. Being unbiased also does not guarantee the smallest mean squared error.

paragraphs.heading: The sample variance
paragraphs.text: One example is the sample variance. The naive version, which divides by n, comes out too low on average, because the sample mean it relies on is worked out from the same data. Multiplying it by n/(n−1), a fix known as Bessel's correction, gives an unbiased estimator.

paragraphs.heading: Bias and consistency
paragraphs.text: Bias is a separate idea from consistency. A consistent estimator converges in probability to the true value of the parameter, and it may be biased or unbiased. An unbiased estimator does not always exist. For instance, if a binomial random variable has parameter p, no unbiased estimator exists for 1/p.

paragraphs.heading: Transforming an estimate
paragraphs.text: Unbiasedness does not always carry over when you transform an estimate. If θ̂ is an unbiased estimator of θ, then g(θ̂) is not guaranteed in general to be unbiased for g(θ), unless g is a linear function. So mean-unbiasedness is lost under non-linear transformations.

paragraphs.heading: Tickets in a box
paragraphs.text: The bias of maximum-likelihood estimators can be large. Suppose tickets numbered 1 to n sit in a box, and you draw one at random and read its number, X. If n is unknown, the maximum-likelihood estimate of n is simply X, even though X is only (n + 1)/2 on average. All you know for certain is that n is at least X, and it is probably more. The natural unbiased estimator here is 2X − 1.

paragraphs.heading: Median-unbiased estimators
paragraphs.text: Bias can also be measured against the median instead of the mean. An estimate is median-unbiased if the median of its distribution sits at the true value, so it underestimates just as often as it overestimates. Such estimators stay median-unbiased under one-to-one transformations. They also exist in some cases where neither a mean-unbiased nor a maximum-likelihood estimator can be found.
